newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria avoids power cuts as miners end strike.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria avoids power cuts as miners end strike.

text.p: Most Bulgarian coal miners, who halted production for four days and depleted coal stocks for thermal power stations, ended a strike on Wednesday after the ruling ex-communists agreed to early elections in April.
Senior energy officials said power cuts and power rationing were inevitable if the miners' strike continued for another week. Coal-fired power stations provide half of the country's electricity.

Work has been resumed in most of Bulgaria's mines, except in those in Pernik and Bobov Dol where strikers want higher wages, Coal Holding firm officials said. The recent strikes had been a heavy blow to the crippled mining sector.
Coal Holding director Dimitar Alexandrov told Reuters the strike had hit the performance of a financial stabilisation programme.
"Under the programme we are trying to help some underground mines survive which face closures," he said. The mines are both inefficient and loss-making.
Bulgaria's biggest Maritsa East mining complex, which produces 30 percent of the country's power, restarted work on Tuesday after early elections were agreed.
"Now we have to compensate a drastic reduction of coal in stock, which now is 700,000 tonnes," the executive director of the Maritsa East complex Yordan Dimov said by telephone.
Dimov said the complex had lost some 350 million levs per day during the miners strike only from missed coal sales. The remaining losses would be difficult to calculate, he added.
Bulgaria, which imports 86 percent of its energy resources, relied on its 3,760-megawatt nuclear power plant for half of its electricity needs during the miners strike.
"All six reactors of the plant are producing a total of 3,200 megawatts, providing half of the country's electricity needs," Kiril Nikolov, chairman of the Kozloduy plant, said by telephone.
Energy Ministry officials said the strike did not affect its contracted obligations for electricity exports of 300-400 megawatts to Turkey.

The energy sector, hamstrung by the headlong fall of the lev, is struggling to survive while the country plunges into hyper-inflation through hard currency profit from exporting electricity when free capacity is available.
The Bulgarian lev traded at 2,700 per dollar from 600 at the beginning of January.
